newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr weathers long-awaited rate cut.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr weathers long-awaited rate cut.

text.p: The Australian dollar rallied 1/3 cent Wednesday as weeks of worry over rates gave way to relief when the Reserve Bank trimmed by only 0.5 point to 6.5 percent.
Indirect support was also derived from a market-favourable status quo result from the U.S. election which propelled the U.S. dollar sharply high, dragging the A$ along for the rise.

"As far as the dollar is concerned, relatively strong interest differential support remains even after the rate cut," said Stephen Roberts, an economist at UBS Australia. "That should keep it above 79 cents for now."
By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the dollar was resting comfortably at US$0.7907/12 after rising from US$0.7865/70 just before the RBA's decision flashed on dealing screens and US$0.7861/66 late here Tuesday.
The reaction was even more enthusiastic on the crosses where it jumped to 90.40/50 yen from 89.44/54 late Tuesday and to 58.6 on its trade weighted index from 58.2.

It took a cue from its U.S. counterpart which rallied to 114.35 yen from 113.80 when the U.S. election produced the market's prefered result -- a win by Democratic incumbent Bill Clinton but continued control of Congress by the Republicans.
There had been concerns the Democrats would sweep Congress and return to the bad old days of spend and borrow.

For domestic investors the main concern, as it had been for weeks, was monetary policy and it looked like remaining an obsession for months to come with the market already pricing in a third easing in the cycle.
The futures market saw scope for a move by March and pushed the 90-day bank bill contract eight basis points higher to 93.83, implying an interest rate of 6.17 percent.
The yield on the 10-yr government bonds subsided another 10 basis points to a fresh 2-1/2 year low of 7.19 percent.

That decline still left Australian bonds with a fat yield premium of 469 basis points over their Japanese counterparts, which analysts felt would sustain the recent burst of demand for yen/A$ dual currency samurai bonds. Around 135 billion yen of bonds were launched last week and more were expected short term.
In any case, some saw reason to believe that factors like yields and commodity prices were not the Achilles' heel of yore.

"Conventional wisdom would suggest the narrowing in rate differentials and the recent dip in commodity prices would see the A$ significantly lower than present," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
"But a vontinued re-rating of Australia from offshore on the sound fundamentals plus the diversification of the export base away from commodities, are underpinning the A$," he said.
A sustained uptrend past 80 cents looked unlikely, however, given that speculation of yet another policy easing lay like a cloud on the horizon.
The RBA itself skirted around the issue in the statement which accompanied the cut but did link the move to inflation rather than any particular worries about economic growth.
It also warned that some enterprise were agreements were too high and the moderation in broad pay deals may not last.
Bruce Freeland, chief economist at Commonwealth Bank, said it was clear the RBA remained confident economic growth would pick-up in 1997, a sentiment he shared.

"As such, we do not expect any further rate cuts in the current cycle," he said. "At the very least, the RBA can be expected to sit back and watch the run of indicators over the next few months before making any further decision."

The first of those figures comes Thursday with the release of October jobs data. Median forecasts are for employment to bounce back by 12,000 after September's sharp 34,100 drop, with unemployment steady at 8.7 pct. -- Sydney newsroom 61-2 373 1800
